title: landau-windows-acl2 — how much foundation does a proof need?

segments.text: A proof of the Riemann hypothesis has recently been checked in Lean. Independent programs have accepted the formal proof. It concerns one of the most famous questions about the pattern of prime numbers. That is a remarkable development. But it leaves another question. How much mathematical machinery does this particular argument really need? To explain what Landau Windows A C L two is trying to do, we need to look at the foundations underneath a proof.

segments.chapter: Peano arithmetic: rules about whole numbers
segments.text: Start with the whole numbers. Zero, one, two, three, and so on. Peano arithmetic is a precise system of rules about those numbers. It tells us how the next number works, and how addition and multiplication behave. It also gives us induction. Imagine a row of dominoes. Establish the first case, then show that whenever one case holds, the next one holds too. Together, those two steps prove the property for every whole number. We never have to check the numbers one at a time. Arithmetic can also encode finite lists, fractions, and the steps of a calculation. So this small starting point can express a surprising amount of mathematics.

Now give ourselves a larger framework. Z F C is a standard collection of rules for set theory. A set is a collection of mathematical objects. The rules let us build new sets, work with infinite sets, and develop a great deal of ordinary mathematics. Even the whole numbers can be built out of sets. We can start with the empty set, then build a sequence representing zero, one, two, and so on. Inside this framework we can also construct functions, real numbers, and spaces. That is one reason Z F C is stronger than Peano arithmetic. It can describe and justify much more than the arithmetic rules alone.

Why does the strength of the rules matter? First, we need a word: consistency. A consistent system never proves a contradiction, such as zero equals one. Checking a particular proof is a finite task. But saying that no proof of a contradiction exists is a statement about every possible proof. There is a remarkable connection here. A finite proof can itself be encoded as a whole number. That lets arithmetic make statements about proofs. In nineteen thirty one, Godel established his second incompleteness theorem. Under its usual conditions, a consistent system with mechanically specified rules and enough arithmetic cannot prove its own formal consistency. This applies to Peano arithmetic, and to Z F C. So a system can check individual arguments without being able to establish, from its own rules, that those rules will never produce a contradiction.

A stronger system can sometimes provide that justification for a weaker one. Here is how Z F C does it for Peano arithmetic. It constructs the whole numbers, together with addition and multiplication, and checks that they satisfy the arithmetic axioms. This is called building a model: a mathematical world where the rules hold. Valid proof steps preserve truth in that world. So an arithmetic proof cannot lead from those rules to a contradiction. That gives a proof of the consistency of Peano arithmetic, carried out inside Z F C. The justification depends on the stronger framework. When Z F C asks about its own consistency, Godel's limit still applies.

Now repeat that idea one level higher. Not all infinities have the same size. An inaccessible cardinal is a special size of infinity with a useful feature for our story. If one exists, the sets below it form a mathematical world satisfying Z F C. So assuming such a cardinal exists gives us a way to prove that Z F C is consistent. But we just met the obstacle. If Z F C is consistent, it cannot prove its own consistency. Therefore it cannot prove that an inaccessible cardinal exists, either. If it could, the model we just described would supply the forbidden consistency proof. Accepting an inaccessible cardinal is therefore an additional assumption beyond Z F C. This is why reducing the assumptions behind a theorem is a meaningful mathematical goal. We want to understand exactly how much of this larger framework the argument actually needs.

segments.chapter: What does this proof actually need?
segments.text: Return to Lean. A standard way to model its hierarchy of universes uses set theory together with inaccessible cardinals. This describes a powerful background available to the system. But the Riemann hypothesis has formulations entirely about whole numbers. That doesn't mean it can be proved using only rules about whole numbers. But it raises a useful question: how much of the proof can be brought down to that level? We can investigate one piece at a time. Proving the same conclusion from fewer assumptions reduces what we have to accept in order to obtain that result.

To see which piece we are studying, return to the picture from the original video. The dots are zeros of the zeta function, and the Riemann hypothesis puts them on the central line. There is a mirror symmetry. An off-centre dot on the left would have a partner on the right. So ruling out dots on the right is enough.

Now watch the gap: the difference between a weighted prime count and its prediction. If a zero sits too far to the right, it contributes an oscillation that grows too quickly. That extra wave rises and falls. Eventually it would drive the gap above the allowed level. Now suppose we could prove an upper bound that the gap never crosses. Then that troublesome zero could not be there. We only used a ceiling; a matching lower bound was unnecessary. Landau's theorem makes that reasoning rigorous. In the larger proof, another argument supplies the ceiling. This connection between a one sided bound and a zero free region is the bridge we want to extract.

This is our part of the picture. It is a classical theorem with a clear input and a clear output. That makes it a natural place to start reducing the foundations. Constructing the ceiling is a different, much larger task. We are isolating this conversion step.

segments.chapter: A finite witness inside a window
segments.text: Our version only gets the ceiling on recurring stretches of the number line, called windows. A zero in the forbidden region must eventually force a violation in sufficiently large windows. The effective theorem should compute where that violation happens, and certify it with exact bounds. So the goal includes both finding a witness and proving that the search succeeds under the intended hypotheses.

We will use A C L two, a proof system based on a computational logic for applicative Common Lisp. Common Lisp is its programming language. The foundational issue is the logical rules we use. We can express our calculations with finite lists, exact fractions, and recursive functions, then prove their properties by induction. That brings us back to the whole number reasoning we started with. The target is a proof at roughly Peano arithmetic strength, with that connection made precise.

That is what Landau Windows A C L two is for. Take this one bridge, extract its finite content, and prove the whole reduction. The general theorem must include a proof that the search succeeds, together with its connection to the original mathematics. That full arithmetic reduction is still in progress. The aim is simple: the same mathematical result, with fewer assumptions.
